## Size isn’t everything. But it sure is something.
There’s a specific feeling you get walking into a 100,000-seat stadium for the first time. It’s not awe exactly. More like disbelief. Your brain doesn’t quite accept that a space this large was built by humans, for humans, to watch other humans play a game.
But here’s the thing most “biggest stadiums” lists get wrong: they treat capacity as a simple number. It’s not. A stadium’s official capacity changes over time. Seats get added, sections get converted to premium suites, standing areas get replaced with bucket seats. The number you see on Wikipedia today might be different from the one you’d see next year.
So here’s our 2026 ranking of the largest stadiums in the world by capacity: not just the numbers, but the stories behind them.

## Size isn’t everything. But it sure is something.
> **The 20 largest stadiums in the world by capacity (2026 ranking):**  
>   
>   
> 1.   **Narendra Modi Stadium**: 132,000 (Ahmedabad, India)  
> 2.   **Rungrado May Day Stadium**: 113,281 (Pyongyang, North Korea)  
> 3.   **Michigan Stadium**: 107,601 (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)  
> 4.   **Beaver Stadium**: 106,572 (University Park, Pennsylvania, USA)  
> 5.   **Ohio Stadium**: 102,780 (Columbus, Ohio, USA)  
> 6.   **Kyle Field**: 102,733 (College Station, Texas, USA)  
> 7.   **Tiger Stadium**: 102,321 (Baton Rouge, Louisiana, USA)  
> 8.   **Neyland Stadium**: 101,915 (Knoxville, Tennessee, USA)  
> 9.   **Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium**: 100,119 (Austin, Texas, USA)  
> 10.   **Bryant-Denny Stadium**: 100,077 (Tuscaloosa, Alabama, USA)  
> 11.   **Melbourne Cricket Ground**: 100,024 (Melbourne, Australia)  
> 12.   **Camp Nou**: 99,354 (Barcelona, Spain). Europe’s largest, rising to about 105,000 when the Espai Barça rebuild completes.  
> 13.   **Sanford Stadium**: 93,033 (Athens, Georgia, USA)  
> 14.   **Cotton Bowl**: 92,100 (Dallas, Texas, USA)  
> 15.   **Wembley Stadium**: 90,000 (London, England)  
> 16.   **Rose Bowl**: 89,702 (Pasadena, California, USA)  

## Size isn’t everything. But it sure is something.
> 17.   **Lusail Stadium**: 88,966 (Lusail, Qatar). The largest stadium ever built for a World Cup final.  
> 18.   **Ben Hill Griffin Stadium**: 88,548 (Gainesville, Florida, USA)  
> 19.   **Jordan-Hare Stadium**: 88,043 (Auburn, Alabama, USA)  
> 20.   **Estadio Azteca**: 87,523 (Mexico City, Mexico). Latin America’s largest, and host of the 2026 World Cup opener.  
>   
>   
> **Also covered in full below, just outside the top 20:**  
>   
>   
> *   **MetLife Stadium**: 82,500 (East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA). The largest NFL stadium, and host of the 2026 World Cup final.  
> *   **Stade de France**: 81,338 (Saint-Denis, France). The largest stadium in France, and its national stadium since 1998.  
> *   **AT&T Stadium**: 80,000 (Arlington, Texas, USA). Expandable past 100,000 for major events.  
> *   **SoFi Stadium**: 70,240 (Inglewood, California, USA). The most expensive stadium ever built, at roughly $5.5 billion.  
>   
>   
> Full rankings with construction, fan culture, and 2026 context below.
* * *

## 1. Narendra Modi Stadium, 132,000 (Ahmedabad, India)
The world’s actual largest stadium isn’t a football venue. It’s a cricket ground.
Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad holds 132,000 spectators, which makes it not only the world’s largest cricket stadium but the world’s largest stadium of any kind. It opened in its current rebuilt form in 2020, replacing the older Sardar Patel Stadium that occupied the same site since 1982. The complete rebuild was driven by the Gujarat Cricket Association at a cost of around $114 million, and the result is a venue that genuinely changes how you think about what “big” means for a sports facility.
The architecture is striking. A modern oval bowl with two tiers all the way around, an LED-illuminated exterior, four dressing rooms that can host two simultaneous matches, and a 55-meter-wide playing field. When it’s full for an India vs Pakistan cricket match, the noise level is documented to rival anything in football.
Most Western readers underestimate this stadium because cricket coverage in North America and Europe is limited, and the stadium’s name change in 2021 (to honor India’s prime minister) generated political coverage that overshadowed the sporting story. But by capacity, Narendra Modi Stadium sits comfortably above every other stadium on Earth, about 19,000 seats clear of the next-largest venue.
> **132,000 seats**: Narendra Modi Stadium is the largest sports venue in the world by capacity, roughly 19,000 seats above Rungrado May Day Stadium at #2.
* * *

## 2. Rungrado May Day Stadium, 113,281 (Pyongyang, North Korea)
The biggest stadium in the football world is one almost nobody reading this will ever visit.
Rungrado May Day Stadium in Pyongyang has held the top football-capacity spot since it opened in 1989. Its official capacity is 113,281, though some sources have questioned whether that number reflects reality. The stadium was originally built for the 13th World Festival of Youth and Students, and its scalloped roof design (16 arches meant to resemble a magnolia blossom) is genuinely striking.
Here’s what makes it strange, though. Rungrado isn’t really used as a sports venue anymore. It hosts the Mass Games, North Korea’s massive choreographed propaganda spectacle, and the occasional political rally. Satellite imagery suggests it’s gone through periods of disrepair. Football matches have been played there, but irregularly.
So yes, it’s technically the second-largest stadium in the world and the largest football venue. But it’s also arguably the least accessible and least active stadium on this entire list. Make of that what you will.
> **113,281 seats**: Rungrado May Day Stadium in Pyongyang has held the world’s largest football-stadium spot since 1989, though its actual regular attendance remains a mystery.
* * *

## 3. Michigan Stadium, 107,601 (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
“The Big House” earns its nickname every single Saturday in the fall.
Michigan Stadium’s capacity of 107,601 makes it the largest stadium in the Western world and the third-largest on Earth. And unlike Rungrado, this place actually fills up. Regularly. Michigan Wolverines football games routinely draw crowds that exceed the official capacity, with the all-time on-campus attendance record sitting at 115,109 (set during a 2013 game against Notre Dame).
What’s wild about Michigan Stadium is how it achieves its size. The bowl sits mostly below ground level, so from the outside, it doesn’t look nearly as massive as it is. You walk in at what feels like ground level and realize you’re standing near the top of the upper deck. It’s a clever bit of engineering from 1927 that still works beautifully.
The Big House is also a reminder that American college football operates on a scale that baffles most of the world. A university (not a professional franchise, not a national team) fills a 107,000-seat stadium eight times a year. That’s just how it works in Ann Arbor.
* * *

## 4. Beaver Stadium, 106,572 (University Park, Pennsylvania, USA)
Penn State’s Beaver Stadium is in the middle of its own renovation story, but even before the current project, it held 106,572 fans. That puts it in a dead heat with some of the other American college giants.
What makes Beaver Stadium distinctive is the atmosphere. “White Out” games, where the entire stadium wears white, are genuinely one of the most visually striking things in all of sports. Over 100,000 people, all in white, in a stadium surrounded by nothing but central Pennsylvania farmland. It’s surreal.
The ongoing renovation is expected to reduce capacity somewhat while adding modern amenities. That’s a trend we’ll talk about more at the end of this list.
* * *

## 5. Ohio Stadium, 102,780 (Columbus, Ohio, USA)
“The Horseshoe” opened in 1922, and Ohio State has been packing it ever since.
With 102,780 seats, Ohio Stadium is another college football cathedral that would rank among the largest professional venues in the world if it were used for anything other than Buckeyes games. The open end of the horseshoe shape gives it one of the most recognizable silhouettes in American sports.
Ohio State has sold out every home game since 1964. That’s six decades of 100,000+ attendance. Every. Single. Game.
* * *

## 6. Kyle Field, 102,733 (College Station, Texas, USA)
Texas A&M’s Kyle Field is loud. Unreasonably loud.
At 102,733, it’s the largest stadium in the SEC (Southeastern Conference) and one of the most intimidating environments in college football. The “12th Man” tradition, where the entire student section stands for the full game, creates a wall of noise that visiting teams genuinely dread.
Kyle Field got a massive renovation in 2015 that pushed its capacity past the 100,000 mark. The Aggies spent over $450 million on it, and the result is a stadium that combines old-school college atmosphere with modern infrastructure.
* * *

## 7. Tiger Stadium, 102,321 (Baton Rouge, Louisiana, USA)
“Death Valley” at LSU sits at 102,321, putting it eighth in the world by capacity. Tiger Stadium is known for producing some of the highest decibel readings ever recorded at a sporting event.
When LSU plays a night game (and it’s always better at night in Baton Rouge), the noise literally registers on seismographs. That’s not an exaggeration. Geologists at LSU have measured it.
* * *

## 8. Neyland Stadium, 101,915 (Knoxville, Tennessee, USA)
Yes, another American college stadium. I know. But the numbers don’t lie.
Neyland Stadium holds 101,915 for Tennessee Volunteers football, and its location on the banks of the Tennessee River makes it one of the most scenic major stadiums anywhere. The “Vol Navy” (fans who arrive by boat and dock along the river) is one of the best tailgating traditions in college football.
The stadium’s capacity has actually decreased from its peak. At one point, Neyland held over 104,000. The reduction came from adding wider seats and more premium areas. Again, a trend worth noting.
> **12 stadiums above 100,000**: Of the world’s top 12 stadiums by capacity, eight are American college football venues. The remaining four span North Korea, Spain, India, and Australia, in sports ranging from football to cricket.
* * *

## 9. Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium, 100,119 (Austin, Texas, USA)
The University of Texas at Austin plays football at DKR-Texas Memorial Stadium, which holds 100,119 after the most recent expansion. Named for legendary coach Darrell K Royal, the stadium opened in 1924 and has been expanded multiple times to its current capacity.
Texas joined the SEC in 2024, which intensified rivalry games that already drew capacity crowds. The atmosphere on a fall Saturday in Austin combines college football scale with the city’s broader live-music energy. The result is one of the more distinctive game-day experiences in the sport.
The stadium underwent another expansion in the late 2010s that added premium seating in the south end zone. The headline capacity sits at 100,119, but the venue has hosted 102,000+ crowds for marquee matchups.
* * *

## 10. Bryant-Denny Stadium, 100,077 (Tuscaloosa, Alabama, USA)
Bryant-Denny Stadium holds 100,077 and is the home of Alabama Crimson Tide football. Named for legendary coach Paul “Bear” Bryant and former university president George H. Denny, the stadium opened in 1929 and has been expanded continuously over nearly a century.
What makes Bryant-Denny remarkable isn’t just its size. It’s the sustained success the program has had inside it. Alabama has won multiple national championships in the 21st century alone, and home games regularly run at full capacity even for non-conference opponents.
The atmosphere at a night game against an SEC West rival is among the most intense in American sports. The combination of Southern football culture, decades of accumulated tradition, and the team’s modern-era dominance creates a venue experience that visiting programs talk about for years.
* * *

## 1. Narendra Modi Stadium, 132,000 (Ahmedabad, India)
The world’s actual largest stadium isn’t a football venue. It’s a cricket ground.
Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad holds 132,000 spectators, which makes it not only the world’s largest cricket stadium but the world’s largest stadium of any kind. It opened in its current rebuilt form in 2020, replacing the older Sardar Patel Stadium that occupied the same site since 1982. The complete rebuild was driven by the Gujarat Cricket Association at a cost of around $114 million, and the result is a venue that genuinely changes how you think about what “big” means for a sports facility.
The architecture is striking. A modern oval bowl with two tiers all the way around, an LED-illuminated exterior, four dressing rooms that can host two simultaneous matches, and a 55-meter-wide playing field. When it’s full for an India vs Pakistan cricket match, the noise level is documented to rival anything in football.
Most Western readers underestimate this stadium because cricket coverage in North America and Europe is limited, and the stadium’s name change in 2021 (to honor India’s prime minister) generated political coverage that overshadowed the sporting story. But by capacity, Narendra Modi Stadium sits comfortably above every other stadium on Earth, about 19,000 seats clear of the next-largest venue.
> **132,000 seats**: Narendra Modi Stadium is the largest sports venue in the world by capacity, roughly 19,000 seats above Rungrado May Day Stadium at #2.

## 2. Rungrado May Day Stadium, 113,281 (Pyongyang, North Korea)
The biggest stadium in the football world is one almost nobody reading this will ever visit.
Rungrado May Day Stadium in Pyongyang has held the top football-capacity spot since it opened in 1989. Its official capacity is 113,281, though some sources have questioned whether that number reflects reality. The stadium was originally built for the 13th World Festival of Youth and Students, and its scalloped roof design (16 arches meant to resemble a magnolia blossom) is genuinely striking.
Here’s what makes it strange, though. Rungrado isn’t really used as a sports venue anymore. It hosts the Mass Games, North Korea’s massive choreographed propaganda spectacle, and the occasional political rally. Satellite imagery suggests it’s gone through periods of disrepair. Football matches have been played there, but irregularly.
So yes, it’s technically the second-largest stadium in the world and the largest football venue. But it’s also arguably the least accessible and least active stadium on this entire list. Make of that what you will.
> **113,281 seats**: Rungrado May Day Stadium in Pyongyang has held the world’s largest football-stadium spot since 1989, though its actual regular attendance remains a mystery.
* * *

## 3. Michigan Stadium, 107,601 (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
“The Big House” earns its nickname every single Saturday in the fall.
Michigan Stadium’s capacity of 107,601 makes it the largest stadium in the Western world and the third-largest on Earth. And unlike Rungrado, this place actually fills up. Regularly. Michigan Wolverines football games routinely draw crowds that exceed the official capacity, with the all-time on-campus attendance record sitting at 115,109 (set during a 2013 game against Notre Dame).
What’s wild about Michigan Stadium is how it achieves its size. The bowl sits mostly below ground level, so from the outside, it doesn’t look nearly as massive as it is. You walk in at what feels like ground level and realize you’re standing near the top of the upper deck. It’s a clever bit of engineering from 1927 that still works beautifully.
The Big House is also a reminder that American college football operates on a scale that baffles most of the world. A university (not a professional franchise, not a national team) fills a 107,000-seat stadium eight times a year. That’s just how it works in Ann Arbor.
* * *

## 4. Beaver Stadium, 106,572 (University Park, Pennsylvania, USA)
Penn State’s Beaver Stadium is in the middle of its own renovation story, but even before the current project, it held 106,572 fans. That puts it in a dead heat with some of the other American college giants.
What makes Beaver Stadium distinctive is the atmosphere. “White Out” games, where the entire stadium wears white, are genuinely one of the most visually striking things in all of sports. Over 100,000 people, all in white, in a stadium surrounded by nothing but central Pennsylvania farmland. It’s surreal.
The ongoing renovation is expected to reduce capacity somewhat while adding modern amenities. That’s a trend we’ll talk about more at the end of this list.

“The Horseshoe” opened in 1922, and Ohio State has been packing it ever since.
With 102,780 seats, Ohio Stadium is another college football cathedral that would rank among the largest professional venues in the world if it were used for anything other than Buckeyes games. The open end of the horseshoe shape gives it one of the most recognizable silhouettes in American sports.
Ohio State has sold out every home game since 1964. That’s six decades of 100,000+ attendance. Every. Single. Game.

## 6. Kyle Field, 102,733 (College Station, Texas, USA)
Texas A&M’s Kyle Field is loud. Unreasonably loud.
At 102,733, it’s the largest stadium in the SEC (Southeastern Conference) and one of the most intimidating environments in college football. The “12th Man” tradition, where the entire student section stands for the full game, creates a wall of noise that visiting teams genuinely dread.
Kyle Field got a massive renovation in 2015 that pushed its capacity past the 100,000 mark. The Aggies spent over $450 million on it, and the result is a stadium that combines old-school college atmosphere with modern infrastructure.
* * *

## 7. Tiger Stadium, 102,321 (Baton Rouge, Louisiana, USA)
“Death Valley” at LSU sits at 102,321, putting it eighth in the world by capacity. Tiger Stadium is known for producing some of the highest decibel readings ever recorded at a sporting event.
When LSU plays a night game (and it’s always better at night in Baton Rouge), the noise literally registers on seismographs. That’s not an exaggeration. Geologists at LSU have measured it.
* * *

## 8. Neyland Stadium, 101,915 (Knoxville, Tennessee, USA)
Yes, another American college stadium. I know. But the numbers don’t lie.
Neyland Stadium holds 101,915 for Tennessee Volunteers football, and its location on the banks of the Tennessee River makes it one of the most scenic major stadiums anywhere. The “Vol Navy” (fans who arrive by boat and dock along the river) is one of the best tailgating traditions in college football.
The stadium’s capacity has actually decreased from its peak. At one point, Neyland held over 104,000. The reduction came from adding wider seats and more premium areas. Again, a trend worth noting.

## 9. Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium, 100,119 (Austin, Texas, USA)
The University of Texas at Austin plays football at DKR-Texas Memorial Stadium, which holds 100,119 after the most recent expansion. Named for legendary coach Darrell K Royal, the stadium opened in 1924 and has been expanded multiple times to its current capacity.
Texas joined the SEC in 2024, which intensified rivalry games that already drew capacity crowds. The atmosphere on a fall Saturday in Austin combines college football scale with the city’s broader live-music energy. The result is one of the more distinctive game-day experiences in the sport.
The stadium underwent another expansion in the late 2010s that added premium seating in the south end zone. The headline capacity sits at 100,119, but the venue has hosted 102,000+ crowds for marquee matchups.

## 10. Bryant-Denny Stadium, 100,077 (Tuscaloosa, Alabama, USA)
Bryant-Denny Stadium holds 100,077 and is the home of Alabama Crimson Tide football. Named for legendary coach Paul “Bear” Bryant and former university president George H. Denny, the stadium opened in 1929 and has been expanded continuously over nearly a century.
What makes Bryant-Denny remarkable isn’t just its size. It’s the sustained success the program has had inside it. Alabama has won multiple national championships in the 21st century alone, and home games regularly run at full capacity even for non-conference opponents.
The atmosphere at a night game against an SEC West rival is among the most intense in American sports. The combination of Southern football culture, decades of accumulated tradition, and the team’s modern-era dominance creates a venue experience that visiting programs talk about for years.
